title: As Space Gets Connected, Security Gets Critical
gist: As NASA's LunaNet and commercial satellite constellations bring terrestrial-style connectivity to the moon and orbit, chipmakers (Synopsys, GlobalFoundries, Cadence/Secure-IC, Rambus, Infineon, Microchip) are racing to embed root-of-trust, post-quantum crypto, and rad-tolerant reprogrammable hardware, because physically inaccessible, high-value space assets are prime targets for nation-state ransomware and sabotage, and optical inter-satellite links are displacing RF for security and speed even as they open a new physical attack vector (laser weaponization).

insights.claim: NASA's LunaNet uses Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) as its core network framework to keep signal integrity between rovers, astronauts, satellites, and Earth despite the inherent latency of moon-to-Earth distances.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: DTN becomes a foundational protocol layer that space-hardware vendors (radio, compute, security IP) must design around; expect DTN-compatible chipsets to become a checkbox requirement for lunar/deep-space contracts.
insights.quote: NASA’s lunar network will leverage Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking to maintain signal integrity between rovers, astronauts, satellites, and more.

insights.claim: NASA's current lunar radio vendor is Nokia, running LTE consistent with later 4G nodes, and NASA is still evaluating whether 5G equipment is mature enough to upgrade to, prioritizing first establishing basic surface-to-Earth connectivity for both government and commercial vehicles.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Nokia has an incumbent position in lunar network infrastructure; a NASA decision to move to 5G would be a signal for follow-on contract activity and for chip vendors supplying 5G security IP (stronger mutual authentication, zero-trust architecture) into space-rated hardware.
insights.quote: NASA’s vendor for those radios is Nokia, and they are using LTE systems that are consistent with the later 4G technology nodes
insights.locator: Shawn Carpenter quote on NASA vendor

insights.claim: 4G remains the lower-risk deployment choice for lunar networks today because it is a more mature ecosystem, even though 5G adds meaningful security upgrades such as stronger mutual authentication and zero-trust-oriented network slicing for mission segmentation.
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys
insights.so_what: The 4G-vs-5G tradeoff in space is a proxy for a broader pattern: mission-critical/high-value programs favor mature over cutting-edge tech until security features can be proven, which slows adoption curves for newer RF/security IP vendors targeting aerospace.

insights.claim: Satellite-based 5G millimeter-wave communication inverts the terrestrial line-of-sight limitation into an advantage by beaming directly from orbit into user terminals and ground stations via beamforming.
insights.speaker: Shankaran Janardhanan, senior vice president of RF at GlobalFoundries
insights.so_what: Reframes satellite-direct-to-device as a structural workaround for a terrestrial 5G mmWave weakness, supporting continued capex into satellite beamforming RF front-ends (an area GlobalFoundries and peers supply).
insights.quote: The satellite format has flipped the problem on its head

insights.claim: GlobalFoundries is bringing to market one of the first eight-inch (vs. the industry-standard six-inch) high-volume gallium nitride-on-silicon technologies manufactured in the U.S., aimed at the satellite power-amplifier market.
insights.speaker: Shankaran Janardhanan, senior vice president of RF at GlobalFoundries
insights.so_what: A U.S.-manufactured, larger-wafer GaN process is both a cost/yield advantage over incumbent six-inch GaN and a national-security selling point (closed-loop, domestically built supply chain) — watch for GF design wins in satellite power amplifiers and any CHIPS Act-linked funding.
insights.quote: GF’s gallium nitride on silicon is going to be one of the first eight-inch high-volume gallium nitride silicon technologies that’s manufactured in the U.S. This is a very important thing

themes.theme: Space as a new attack surface

insights.claim: Nation states are described as the number one, best-funded, most determined threat actors targeting satellites, motivated by both economic and diplomatic/strategic value, and this dynamic is explicitly cited as part of the rationale behind government programs like the CHIPS Act.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Ties satellite/space hardware security spend directly to geopolitical competition and government funding flows — a durable, policy-backed demand driver for security-IP vendors (Secure-IC, Rambus, Synopsys) selling into aerospace.
insights.quote: The number one threat, and the most funded, most determined threats, are nation states. That’s real and is also the reason we have the CHIPS Act and other government programs.

insights.claim: An adversary who compromises control of an inter-satellite laser link could increase its power to physically burn sensors or destroy satellites, since in free space at 400-600 km lasers remain extremely tightly focused with very high watts-per-square-millimeter density.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Optical links, marketed as an anti-eavesdropping upgrade over RF, carry a distinct kinetic-weaponization risk if command/control is hijacked — a second-order security requirement (power-limiting, authentication on beam-steering commands) that vendors need to design in, not just encryption.
insights.quote: In free space, when you are 400 to 500 to 600 kilometers away, you’re almost outside of the atmosphere, so your lasers go almost straight

insights.claim: Attackers targeting space and satellite networks are often financially motivated via denial-of-service/ransomware extraction rather than caring about the data itself.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel, director of strategic programs, security, processor, wireless and NVM at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Reframes the primary commercial-satellite threat model away from espionage toward extortion economics — implies demand for availability-focused hardening (redundant links, fast recovery) as much as confidentiality tooling.
insights.quote: If hackers can create a denial-of-service attack, they can charge you a nice tidy sum. They don’t care about the data as much as they care about extracting it away to ransomware your device.

insights.claim: A large-scale nuclear detonation in space could trigger an EMP event capable of frying most commercial satellites, while government satellites are hardened to survive such radiation/stress levels.
insights.speaker: Helmut Puchner, fellow and VP of Aerospace and Defense at Infineon Technologies
insights.so_what: Highlights an asymmetric resilience gap between government and commercial satellite fleets that insurers, commercial operators, and radiation-hardening chip suppliers (Infineon, Microchip) should be pricing into risk models.
insights.quote: But if somebody triggers a nuclear event in space, I was told it populates around the globe in space and causes an EMP (electromagnetic pulse) event that might fry all the commercial satellites. Not the government ones, because they are built to sustain those levels of radiation or stress, but the commercial ones will not survive.

themes.theme: Optical links vs. RF: security and performance tradeoffs

insights.claim: Laser-based optical inter-satellite links (OISLs) transmit data at up to 100x the rate of traditional RF and are immune to electronic jamming, but their narrow, precisely pointed beams make interception require physical line-of-sight positioning that is itself detectable.
insights.speaker: Dalius Petrulionis, CTO at Astrolight
insights.so_what: The 100x bandwidth-and-stealth combination positions OISLs as the emerging default for high-value, high-security space links (military, orbital data-center GPU interconnect) over legacy RF — a tailwind for optical-communication component suppliers.
insights.quote: Laser communication is a line-of-sight technology that uses narrow, focused beams of infrared light to transmit data at up to 100X faster rates than traditional RF.

insights.claim: Combining quantum key distribution (QKD) over the optical channel with a classical encrypted channel gives physically provable security, because eavesdropping attempts perturb the precisely pointed laser link in a detectable way.
insights.speaker: Dalius Petrulionis, CTO at Astrolight
insights.so_what: QKD-over-laser is presented as a defense against future quantum-computer-broken RF encryption — an early-stage but potentially critical differentiator for optical comms vendors selling into defense/space as quantum-computing threats mature.
insights.quote: We have quantum key distribution using the same optical medium, which you can’t do over RF, and we combine that with a classical channel

insights.claim: NASA's Psyche mission already demonstrates optical links beaming data directly from the asteroid belt to Earth without relay intermediaries, and the Artemis lunar mission used optical connectivity to transmit huge data volumes, showing OISL is a proven, not merely theoretical, capability.
insights.speaker: Dalius Petrulionis, CTO at Astrolight
insights.so_what: Flight heritage on deep-space optical links (Psyche, Artemis) de-risks the technology for near-term commercial adoption, supporting the case that optical will keep taking share from RF for high-value long-haul space data.
insights.quote: There’s a NASA Psyche mission that beams data from the asteroid belt, which is orders of magnitude further away, down to Earth without any intermediaries

insights.claim: Optical connectivity is expected to be preferred over RF for very high-speed inter-satellite links and for connecting GPUs within orbital data centers, while RF remains the choice for satellite-to-ground-terminal links where downlink signal quality suffices.
insights.speaker: Shankaran Janardhanan, senior vice president of RF at GlobalFoundries
insights.so_what: Signals a durable market segmentation — optical for satellite-to-satellite/orbital-compute backhaul, RF for the last hop to ground — useful for positioning bets across both silicon photonics and RF GaN/SiGe suppliers rather than picking one winner.
insights.locator: Janardhanan on optical vs RF use cases

insights.claim: The moving, unpredictable positions of satellites in orbit make it harder to trace where data is physically hopping, which could be exploited to perform confidential computation in a jurisdictionally neutral, extraterritorial space environment.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A speculative but investor-relevant angle: space-based compute could be marketed not just for connectivity but as a jurisdiction-neutral computation venue for extremely sensitive data, a novel demand driver for orbital data center players beyond the 'edge compute' narrative.
insights.quote: It might be another way to evade and to do some kind of furtive computation if you have some extremely critical data and you want to reduce the risk of interception or adverse manipulation, especially in the context of nation states. You want to be in a neutral space, extraterritorially, so the jurisdictions do not apply

themes.theme: Hardware root of trust and future-proofing firmware

insights.claim: Space systems require a root of trust with post-quantum cryptography using long keys and multiple algorithm families simultaneously, because if a single PQC algorithm family (e.g., lattice-based schemes) is later broken, the whole system must not fail.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: 'Crypto agility' — running multiple non-overlapping PQC families in parallel — becomes a design requirement, not an option, for any long-lived space asset; security IP vendors that ship multi-algorithm PQC stacks (vs. single-algorithm) have a structural edge in aerospace RFPs.
insights.quote: The root of trust is immutable, meaning you cannot go beneath the root of trust, so it must be future-proof.
insights.locator: Guilley on root of trust and PQC

insights.claim: China is actively working to find vulnerabilities in lattice-based post-quantum cryptography, which is why NIST standardized a non-lattice-based alternative, HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), specifically for algorithmic diversity.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A concrete geopolitical/cryptographic risk: designers relying solely on lattice-based PQC (the current default in many stacks) may be exposed if China's cryptanalysis succeeds — NIST's HQC standardization is a hedging signal worth tracking for compliance requirements in defense-adjacent chip contracts.
insights.quote: China is trying to find vulnerabilities in lattice-based crypto for PQC, so designers are advised to use non-lattice-based schemes
insights.locator: Guilley on China and lattice-based crypto

insights.claim: FPGAs' reprogrammability gives them a structural advantage over ASICs for space assets because firmware, including cryptographic algorithms, can be field-upgraded (e.g., re-flashed to add post-quantum signatures) to fight obsolescence, whereas ASIC-based satellites can become permanently stuck with outdated security.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Favors rad-tolerant FPGA suppliers (Microchip named later in the article) over fixed-function ASIC vendors for long-lifecycle space programs where crypto-agility is now a stated requirement — a durable design-win driver as PQC transitions accelerate.
insights.quote: But if you go with an ASIC or something that is not meant to be future-proof, or upgradable, then you are a bit stuck.
insights.locator: Guilley on FPGA vs ASIC anecdote

insights.claim: In a real-world retrofit with a nanosat company doing radar-photography intelligence collection, an FPGA running Linux was successfully re-flashed to switch from classical crypto signing to post-quantum LMS (Leighton-Micali Hash-Based Signature) signing.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A proof point that PQC retrofits are already operationally viable on deployed satellite hardware today, not just a future roadmap item — relevant for timing PQC-transition-driven IP/tooling revenue for vendors like Secure-IC.
insights.quote: They re-flashed the FPGA, upgraded it, and it worked, signed with LMS (Leighton-Micali Hash-Based Signature), which is a post-quantum crypto.

insights.claim: Physically unclonable function (PUF) key-generation circuits are ideally suited for remote 'key rolling' (updating cryptographic keys on a device even if an adversary has partially compromised it) because the chip-unique transformation function itself is unclonable, even though the generated keys are just ordinary bit strings.
insights.speaker: Scott Best, senior technical director of silicon IP at Rambus
insights.so_what: PUF-based key rolling is positioned as the gold-standard remote key-management mechanism for un-serviceable assets; PUFs are already in production in Microchip's rad-tolerant FPGAs and NASA's rad-hardened RISC-V HPSC-I processors, indicating near-term commercial traction for PUF IP licensors like Rambus.
insights.quote: While the key material they create is not unclonable — keys are just long strings of binary digits, quite easily cloneable — PUFs are ideally suited for key-rolling purposes

insights.claim: Commercial satellite operators are structurally more incentivized than government programs to fully invest in security because they face shareholder lawsuits and product-liability exposure, whereas government missions may cut security corners under timeline pressure even when security is nominally part of the mission.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel, director of strategic programs, security, processor, wireless and NVM at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Counterintuitively, private-sector satellite programs may end up better-secured than some government missions due to liability exposure — investors evaluating commercial space-security spend should weight legal/liability risk as a demand driver alongside geopolitical threat framing.
insights.quote: With some government projects, there’s a mission, and if the mission includes security, that’s great, but if the timeline doesn’t allow you to do it, they may cut corners more than a commercial company might. A commercial company may have more to lose, because they have shareholder lawsuits and product liability.
insights.locator: Hinkel on commercial vs government incentives
